procedural_history.originating_court: Addl. Principal Judge, Tis Hazari Court, Delhi (Order dated 4.5.2022)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 28.01.2021 in Crl. A. Nos.85 and 86 of 2021 of the Supreme Court of India.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Husband filed criminal revision petition seeking setting aside of ex-parte interim maintenance order which got dismissed in default whereas R-2 also filed criminal revision petition seeking an enhancement and by order dated 7.4.2021, it was enhanced to ₹1,27,500.13.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court initially granted bail to the mother-in-law and father-in-law (Petitioners herein) of the Respondent No.2 herein (hereafter “R2” or “applicant” interchangeably) for offences under 420, 406, 468, 34, 120B of IPC and granted interim maintenance in sum of ₹ 1 Lakh per month. The current application is a miscellaneous application filed in the disposed of criminal appeal. The petitioners are arguing that the divorce decree passed in Australia dissolves the marriage between R2 and his son, therefore, parents-in-law are not liable in this case and the petition filed by R2 against petitioner is not maintainable under Section 19 of Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 as it is not applicable in the present case and the prayer asked is in violation of Section 25 of HMA.

issue.issue_text: Applications filed by the daughter-in-law for recovery of both arrears of maintenance and monthly maintenance.

facts: The daughter-in-law (R2) had a maintenance order against her husband, which was enhanced to ₹1,27,500 per month.
The arrears of maintenance had accumulated to approximately ₹1.25 crore.
Previous attempts to execute the order had failed; the father-in-law was imprisoned for 10 months and three attempts to auction family-owned shops were unsuccessful.
The daughter-in-law argued that all available modes of execution had been exhausted and she was dependent on her widowed mother.
The father-in-law argued that he was not personally liable for the maintenance owed by his son, who is still alive.

The daughter-in-law requested the court to use its powers under Article 142 of the Constitution, pointing out that the father-in-law had previously failed to honor an undertaking given to the court to pay the arrears.
law: The daughter-in-law invoked the Supreme Court's power under Article 142 of the Constitution, which allows the court to pass any order necessary for doing complete justice in a case.
application: The Court observed that standard methods of executing the maintenance order had proven ineffective.
Instead of ruling on the father-in-law's direct liability, the Court focused on finding a practical way to ensure the daughter-in-law received the money she was owed from the family's assets.
The Court bypassed the lower courts' execution process and fashioned its own remedy to enforce the maintenance order directly.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the daughter-in-law's application by ordering a specific, multi-step plan for recovery. It directed the Registrar of the Delhi High Court to sell six specific shops and place the proceeds in a fixed deposit, with the interest to be paid to the daughter-in-law. It also ordered that the attachment of rent from a gym on the property would continue until the father-in-law and his son paid the remaining balance of the ₹1.25 crore arrears.

arguments.issue_text: Applications filed by the daughter-in-law for recovery of both arrears of maintenance and monthly maintenance.
appellant_arguments: The Petitioner (father-in-law) had consented to the attachment of shops to the extent of his son's (the husband's) share.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (daughter-in-law/applicant) filed applications seeking the recovery of arrears of maintenance and ongoing monthly maintenance.

cases.case_name: Chenga Reddy v. State of A.P.
cases.principle: The power under Article 142 is meant to supplement the existing legal framework to do complete justice between parties, not to supplant it. It is intended for situations that cannot be effectively addressed by existing laws and should remain undefined and elastic to be moulded to the given situation.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In the exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 142 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court can hold a third party jointly liable with a judgment debtor to fulfill payment obligations, particularly in cases where the judgment debtor has absconded and the third party has actively facilitated the persistent defiance of the court's orders.
obiter: The power under Article 142 is meant to supplement the existing legal framework to do complete justice between the parties, and not to supplant it.
The power under Article 142 is conceived to meet situations which cannot be effectively and appropriately tackled by the existing provisions of law.
A court of equity must act within permissible limits to prevent injustice and can evolve appropriate remedies to further the cause of justice, forging new tools if necessary.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In light of the persistent defiance of court orders by the husband and the petitioner-father-in-law, and the husband having abandoned the wife and fled the country, the court found it necessary to exercise its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 142 of the Constitution to do complete justice. The court held both the father-in-law and the husband liable for the entire sum of maintenance and, to ensure payment, ordered the sale of six of the father-in-law's shops.
legal_tests_applied: The power under Article 142 of the Constitution of India is meant to supplement the existing legal framework to do complete justice between the parties, and not to supplant it. It is conceived to meet situations which cannot be effectively and appropriately tackled by the existing provisions of law.
why_appellant_lost: There has been a persistent defiance by the husband and the petitioner-father-in-law, who have, through one pretext or another, stalled compliance with the orders of the Supreme Court.
The court held that it is the responsibility of the Petitioner-father-in-law and the husband to fulfill the payment of the entire sum.
The husband has abandoned the wife and virtually fled to Australia, making enforcement against him directly impractical and necessitating action against the available party, the father-in-law.
why_respondent_won: The court acted to provide a remedy for the respondent's applications for recovery of maintenance arrears in a situation that could not be effectively and appropriately tackled by existing provisions of law due to the other parties' defiance.
The court's actions were taken with a view to do complete justice between the parties, which in this case meant ensuring the respondent received the maintenance she was owed.
policy_considerations: A court of equity must so act, within the permissible limits so as to prevent injustice.
“Equity is not past the age of child-bearing” and an eﬀort to do justice between the parties is a compulsion of judicial conscience.

Courts can and should strive to evolve an appropriate remedy, in the facts and circumstances of a given case, so as to further the cause of justice, within the available range and forging new tools for the said purpose, if necessary to chisel hard edges of the law.
